title: General Liability Insurance for Small Business: Coverage, Cost and How to Buy
seoTitle: General Liability Insurance: Simple 2026 Guide
excerpt: What general liability insurance covers for a small business, what it leaves out, what it costs in 2026 and how to buy the right policy with confidence.
content:
General liability insurance pays for claims that your business caused injury to someone else or damaged their property, plus your legal defense. Clients and landlords ask for it more than any other cover. The U.S. Small Business Administration says any business may need it. This guide shows what the policy covers, what it leaves out, what it costs and how to buy one.

Key takeaways

  • General liability covers third-party bodily injury, property damage, and personal and advertising injury, plus legal defense costs.
  • It does not cover your own employees, your own property, professional mistakes or vehicles; those need other policies.
  • Small businesses with Insureon paid a median of about $45 a month in 2026, but your price depends on your industry, location and limits.

This article is general information, not insurance or legal advice. Coverage depends on the exact policy wording and your state. Speak to a licensed insurance agent or broker before you buy or change a policy.

What general liability insurance covers

A standard commercial general liability (CGL) policy usually covers four things:

  • Bodily injury to other people, such as a customer who slips in your shop.
  • Property damage you cause to someone else's property, such as a contractor who damages a client's floor.
  • Personal and advertising injury, such as claims of libel, slander or copying someone's advertising.
  • Legal defense costs for a covered claim, even one that turns out to be false.

The ad part matters for any business that markets itself. Say someone claims your ad used their slogan, photo or brand name. That claim may fall under this cover, based on your policy. It is still far better to use only content you own or have paid to use.

What general liability does not cover

Policies also leave out harm you cause on purpose and fines in your contracts. Many limit cover for some trades. Read the list of what is not covered, or ask your agent to walk you through it.

Who needs general liability cover?

The SBA's business insurance guide lists general liability as coverage any business may need. You are especially likely to need it if:

  • Customers or suppliers visit your premises.
  • You work at clients' homes or sites, as contractors, cleaners and installers do.
  • A landlord, client or contract asks for a certificate of insurance.
  • You advertise, run a website or post on social media.

Businesses with employees also need workers' compensation in most states, and the rules are set by each state. General liability does not replace it.

How much does general liability insurance cost?

Insureon reported in March 2026 that its small business customers paid a median of about $45 a month for general liability. In the same data:

  • 22% paid less than $30 a month, and 41% paid between $30 and $60.
  • Annual premiums ranged from about $265 to $3,030.
  • 85% chose limits of $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate.

These figures come from one firm's customers, and many of them are low-risk. Treat them as a guide, not a quote. A roofer will pay far more than a consultant who works from home.

What affects your premium

  • Your industry and the work you do.
  • Policy limits and deductible.
  • Your location and state.
  • Number of employees, payroll and annual revenue.
  • The size and condition of your premises.
  • Years in business and your claims history.

Business owner's policy (BOP) vs general liability

A business owner's policy (BOP) bundles general liability with cover for your own building and kit. It often costs less than buying both on their own. The SBA describes it as a package that suits most small business owners. If you own equipment, stock or furniture, ask for a BOP quote alongside a standalone general liability quote.

Occurrence vs claims-made policies

Most policies are written on an occurrence basis. They cover events that happen while the policy is live, even if the claim comes years later. A claims-made policy covers claims made while the policy is live. If you are offered claims-made cover, ask about the start date it looks back to and "tail" cover for when it ends.

How to buy general liability insurance: seven steps

  1. List your risks. Who visits you, where you work and what could go wrong.
  2. Check what clients and landlords require. Note the limits and any "additional insured" wording in your contracts.
  3. Choose limits. $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate is common, but some contracts require more.
  4. Talk to a licensed agent or broker. Independent agents can compare several insurers for you.
  5. Compare at least three quotes. Compare limits, deductibles, exclusions and the insurer's financial strength, not just price.
  6. Ask about a BOP if you also need property cover.
  7. Get your certificate of insurance and review the policy every year, or when your work changes.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Buying the cheapest policy without reading the exclusions.
  • Assuming general liability covers your employees or professional errors.
  • Choosing limits below what your contracts require.
  • Forgetting to update the policy when you add services, staff or locations.
  • Using photos or content in your marketing that you do not have rights to.

Frequently asked questions

Is general liability insurance required by law?

Usually not by law, but clients, landlords and many contracts require it, and some licenses and permits ask for proof of coverage. Workers' compensation, not general liability, is the policy most states require for businesses with employees.

How much general liability cover do I need?

Many small businesses choose $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate, which Insureon says 85% of its customers selected. Check your contracts and leases, because some require higher limits.

Does general liability cover my own injuries?

No. It covers injuries to third parties. Your own injuries are usually covered by health insurance, and your employees' work injuries by workers' compensation.

What is a certificate of insurance?

A certificate of insurance is a one-page document from your insurer or agent that proves you have coverage and shows your limits. Clients and landlords often ask for one before you start work.

Does SEMRS sell insurance?

No. SEMRS is a digital marketing agency and does not sell or arrange insurance. If you are an insurance agency that wants more leads, read our guide to insurance agency marketing or see our pricing.

Running a small business? Read more in the Business Insurance category or our guide to small business loans for marketing.

title: Personal Injury Lawyer Advertising That Works: Channels, Costs and Bar Rules

excerpt: Personal injury lawyer advertising explained: the channels that bring cases, what clicks and leads cost, and the bar rules every ad must follow.
content:
Personal injury lawyer advertising works when it reaches people in the hours and days after an accident, when they search, call and compare firms. The firms that do well pick a few channels, answer the phone fast and track which ads sign cases. This guide covers the main channels, what they cost, how to measure them and the ethics rules your ads must follow.

Key takeaways

  • Injury clients usually search on Google and call within days, so search ads, Local Services Ads and your Business Profile come first.
  • Legal clicks and leads are among the most expensive in Google Ads, so track cost per signed case, not cost per click.
  • Every ad must follow your state bar's advertising rules: no false or misleading claims and no promised results.

This article is general information about marketing, not legal advice. Lawyer advertising rules differ by state, so check your state bar's rules or ask an ethics counsel before you run an ad.

How injury clients choose a lawyer

Most people have never hired a lawyer before their accident. They search on a phone, often from home or a hospital, with words like "car accident lawyer near me". They look at reviews, call two or three firms and hire the one that answers, sounds calm and explains the next step.

That means your advertising has three jobs:

  1. Be visible where people search in the first days.
  2. Earn trust quickly with reviews, clear practice pages and real photos of your team.
  3. Convert the call with fast answers, a friendly intake script and a clear free consultation offer.

The main personal injury lawyer advertising channels

Google Search ads

Search ads show your firm when someone types a specific phrase, such as "truck accident attorney Houston". You choose the keywords, the area and the hours. They are fast to start and easy to measure, but they are costly in legal. In the 2025 Google Ads benchmarks, attorneys and legal services had the highest average cost per click at $8.58, against $5.26 across all industries. The average legal cost per lead was $131.63.

Keep campaigns tight: one case type per ad group, a matching landing page and a long list of negative keywords such as "jobs", "salary" and "free legal aid". Our guide to Google Ads cost shows how to set a budget from the value of a case.

Local Services Ads

Local Services Ads show above normal search ads with a "Google Screened" badge. You pay per lead (a call or message), not per click. Google lists personal injury lawyer services as an eligible category, and your firm must pass Google's screening first. Compare both formats in Local Services Ads vs Google Ads.

Google Business Profile and reviews

Your Business Profile decides whether you appear in the map results. Fill in every field, pick "Personal injury attorney" as the main category, add office photos and ask every satisfied client for a review. Our Google Business Profile guide walks through each step.

SEO and helpful content

Search engine optimization brings calls you do not pay for per click. It takes months, but it keeps working. Build one page for each case type and city you serve, and answer real questions: "How long does a car accident claim take?" or "Who pays my medical bills?" Our guide to law firm SEO covers the full plan.

TV, radio, billboards and social media

Mass media builds name recognition in a market, so callers already know your firm when they search. It costs much more and is harder to track. Use a unique phone number and web address for each campaign so you can see what it brings in. On social media, short videos that explain common questions work better than "call now" posts.

A simple advertising plan for a small injury firm

Start with the channels closest to the moment of need. Add brand advertising only when intake and tracking are working, or you pay to make the phone ring with no way to know what it earned.

What personal injury lawyer advertising costs

Costs depend on your market, case types and competition. A few rules of thumb help:

  • Budget from a signed case, not a click. If one case in ten leads signs, and you can afford $1,500 to sign a case, you can pay up to $150 a lead.
  • Count every cost. Include agency fees, intake staff and call tracking, not only ad spend.
  • Compare channels by cost per signed case. A cheap lead that never signs is not cheap.
  • Expect a learning month. The first weeks of any paid campaign are mostly testing.

Bar rules every injury lawyer ad must follow

Personal injury lawyer advertising is regulated by each state's rules of professional conduct. Most states base their rules on the ABA Model Rules. Model Rule 7.1 bans false or misleading communication about a lawyer's services. Common problems include:

  • Promising results or implying past verdicts mean a new client will win.
  • Using actors or dramatizations without the disclaimers your state requires.
  • Calling yourself a "specialist" without a certification your state recognizes.
  • Paying for referrals outside the limited exceptions in your state's rules.
  • Soliciting accident victims directly by phone or in person, which most states restrict.

Some state bars also want ads filed or kept on record. Keep a copy of every ad, landing page and script with the date it ran.

How to measure your advertising

  1. Use call tracking with a separate number per channel.
  2. Record the source of every new case in your intake software.
  3. Tag links in ads, emails and social posts. Our free UTM builder creates them in seconds.
  4. Review each month: leads, signed cases and cost per signed case by channel.
  5. Move budget toward the channels that sign cases at the lowest cost.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best advertising for personal injury lawyers?

For most firms, Google search ads, Local Services Ads and a strong Business Profile bring the fastest calls, because people search right after an accident. SEO builds lower-cost cases over time. TV and billboards work best for firms that already have intake and tracking in place.

How much do personal injury lawyers spend on advertising?

It varies widely by market. Legal had the highest average Google Ads cost per click in the 2025 benchmarks at $8.58, with an average cost per lead of $131.63. Set your budget from the value of a signed case and the share of leads that sign.

Can lawyers advertise on Facebook and Instagram?

Yes, if the ads follow your state's lawyer advertising rules. Avoid testimonials or results claims your state restricts, and keep a copy of every ad.

Is it legal for a law firm to pay for leads?

Paying for advertising, including pay-per-lead ads such as Local Services Ads, is generally allowed. Paying someone to recommend you is restricted in most states. Check your state's version of Model Rule 7.2.

Can SEMRS run our law firm advertising?

Yes. SEMRS sets up and manages Google Ads and Local Services Ads in accounts your firm owns, with call tracking and a monthly report on cost per lead. See our paid ads services and pricing.

title: Google Ads for Small Business: A Beginner Guide to Your First Campaign
seoTitle: Google Ads for Small Business: Simple 2026 Guide
excerpt: Google Ads for small business in plain steps: how billing works, how to set a budget, build your first search campaign and avoid costly beginner mistakes.
content:
Google Ads for small business can bring calls and enquiries within days, because your ad shows when someone searches for exactly what you sell. You set the budget, pay only when someone clicks and can stop at any time. This beginner guide explains how billing works, how to plan a budget and how to build your first search campaign without wasting money.

Key takeaways

  • Start with one search campaign, a small list of high-intent keywords and one matching landing page.
  • Set conversion tracking before you spend, so you judge ads by leads, not clicks.
  • Your daily budget is an average: Google can spend up to twice it on a busy day but bills no more than 30.4 times it in a month.

How Google Ads works

Google Ads is an auction. When someone searches, Google picks which ads to show and in what order. It looks at your bid, the quality of your ad and landing page, and how relevant they are to the search. You usually pay per click, so an ad that shows but gets no clicks costs nothing.

There are several campaign types. For a small business, start with Search. Search ads answer a need someone is typing right now, such as "emergency plumber Denver" or "tax accountant near me". Display, video and Performance Max campaigns can work later, once you know which searches bring customers.

What Google Ads costs a small business

You choose the budget, so there is no minimum spend. What you pay per click depends on your industry and area. In the 2025 benchmarks, the average cost per click across industries was $5.26 and the average cost per lead was $70.11. Legal, home services and dental clicks cost more than average.

How billing works matters for planning. Google's help page explains that a campaign can spend up to twice its average daily budget on some days. Over a month, it will charge no more than 30.4 times the daily budget. So a $20 daily budget means about $608 a month at most.

Our guide to Google Ads cost shows how to work out a budget from what a customer is worth.

Google Ads for small business: your first campaign

  1. Set up conversion tracking. Track calls, form submissions and bookings. Without it, you cannot tell good keywords from bad ones.
  2. Choose a Search campaign and turn off the Display Network and search partners at first.
  3. Set your location to the area you actually serve, using "presence" (people in the area), not just interest.
  4. Pick 10 to 20 keywords that show buying intent, such as "boiler repair Leeds" or "same day dentist Austin".
  5. Add negative keywords such as "jobs", "free", "DIY" and "course" so you do not pay for the wrong searches.
  6. Write three ads per ad group with the service, the area and a clear next step.
  7. Send clicks to a matching page. A plumber's "boiler repair" ad should land on a boiler repair page with a phone number at the top.
  8. Set a daily budget you can sustain for at least a month, so Google has time to learn.

Keywords and match types

Start with exact and phrase match. Broad match can work with smart bidding and good conversion data, but it spends faster on loosely related searches. Check the search terms report every week and add any irrelevant terms as negatives.

Local ads and free Google tools

Not all Google advertising is paid. A complete Google Business Profile puts you in map results for free, and it often brings more calls than ads for local services. Many service businesses also qualify for Local Services Ads, which charge per lead and carry a Google badge. Our comparison of Local Services Ads vs Google Ads explains when each one fits.

Common beginner mistakes to avoid

  • No conversion tracking. You end up optimizing for clicks that never call.
  • Too many keywords at once. The budget spreads thin and nothing gets enough data.
  • Sending everyone to the home page. Each ad needs a page about that exact service.
  • Accepting every recommendation. Some suggestions raise spend without raising leads. Read each one first.
  • Changing everything daily. Campaigns need one to two weeks of data before big changes.
  • Ignoring the phone. If calls go to voicemail, the best ads in the world will not help.

How to measure results

The best business credit cards for advertising spend pay you back on the ads you already buy, such as Google, Meta and other online ads, without high fees or interest eating the reward.   • If you need time to pay, a 0% intro APR card costs less than any reward is worth.
  • Business cards lack some consumer protections, and most require a personal guarantee.

This article is general information, not financial advice. Card terms change often, so check the issuer's current terms before you apply. SEMRS has no affiliate or paid relationship with any card issuer named here.

Why put advertising on a business card

Ad platforms such as Google Ads and Meta charge a card again and again as you spend. A business card keeps those costs apart from personal spending, gives you one monthly statement and can earn rewards on money you would spend anyway. It also gives you a short grace period: when you pay the full balance by the due date, you usually pay no interest.

The risk is carrying a balance. Card interest rates are high, so interest on unpaid ad spend can cost more than the ads earn.

The three types of business credit cards

Protections business cards do not have

title: Dental Marketing: How Dentists Get New Patients

content:
Dental marketing is how a practice gets found, trusted and booked by new patients, and how it keeps the patients it already has. Most new patients start with a search such as "dentist near me" and choose from the map results, reviews and the practice website. This guide sets out eight ways to win patients, what each costs in time and money, and the privacy and review rules every practice must follow.

Key takeaways

  • Your Google Business Profile, reviews and website decide most first bookings, so fix them before you buy ads.
  • Use paid search for high-value treatments such as implants, Invisalign and emergency care, with one page per treatment.
  • Patient privacy rules and the FTC review rule apply to all dental marketing, including social media.

This article is general information, not legal advice. Patient privacy and advertising rules vary by country and state, so check your dental board's rules and HIPAA guidance before you use patient information in marketing.

How patients choose a dentist

Patients look for three things: a practice close to home or work, good reviews and an easy way to book. Many also check whether you take their insurance, offer evening or weekend hours and treat nervous patients. If your profile and website answer those questions quickly, you win the booking.

8 ways to get new dental patients

1. Complete your Google Business Profile

Choose "Dentist" as the main category and add services such as "Cosmetic dentist" or "Emergency dental service" where they fit. Add hours, insurance plans, accessibility details and real photos of your team and rooms. Our Google Business Profile guide covers every field.

2. Ask every happy patient for a review

Reviews are one of the strongest local signals. Ask in person at checkout, then send a short text or email with a direct link. Our free Google review link generator makes that link in seconds. Reply to every review in a calm, general way, and never confirm that the reviewer is a patient.

3. Build a fast website with one page per treatment

Patients search for treatments, not for "services". Give implants, Invisalign, whitening, children's dentistry and emergency care their own pages. Each page should explain the treatment, what to expect, prices or payment options, and how to book. Keep the site fast on phones and accessible to everyone; our ADA website compliance guide explains what that means.

4. Use local SEO and helpful content

Answer real questions in short articles: "How long does an implant take to heal?" or "What counts as a dental emergency?" Add your city to page titles where it reads naturally. Our guide to SEO for small business explains the basics of dental SEO marketing step by step.

5. Run Google Ads for high-value treatments

Paid search works well for treatments with high value or urgent need. Keep it tight: one campaign per treatment, keywords with the city name, and ads that send people to the matching page. Dental clicks are among the more expensive in local advertising, so track booked appointments, not clicks. Our guide to Google Ads cost explains how to set a budget.

6. Make booking easy

Put the phone number at the top of every page and add online booking if your system allows it. Answer calls quickly, and call back missed calls the same day. Many new patients book with the first practice that answers.

7. Keep patients with email and text reminders

Recall reminders, hygiene appointments and simple newsletters keep chairs full. Get clear consent before you send marketing messages, and keep appointment reminders separate from promotions.

8. Show your team on social media

Short posts about your team, your community and simple care tips build trust. Never post patient photos, X-rays or stories without written authorization.

Dental marketing budget and timeline

Start with the free and low-cost steps, then add ads once your pages and booking process are ready.

Privacy and review rules for dental marketing

Patient privacy. In the US, the HIPAA Privacy Rule generally requires a patient's written authorization before you use their health information for marketing. That includes testimonials, before-and-after photos and stories that identify a patient. The HHS marketing guidance explains the rule.

Reviews. The FTC's Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule took effect on October 21, 2024. It bans fake reviews, buying positive reviews and hiding negative ones. You may ask for honest reviews; you may not reward only good ones. Staff reviews must disclose that the writer works for you.

Claims. Avoid "best dentist in town" or guaranteed results unless you can prove them. Some dental boards also limit how you describe specialties.

How to measure what works

  1. Ask every new patient how they found you and record it.
  2. Use call tracking for ads and your Business Profile.
  3. Track bookings from your website forms.
  4. Review monthly: new patients by source, cost per new patient and recall rates.

For most practices, a complete Google Business Profile, steady reviews and a fast website with treatment pages bring the most new patients for the least money. Google Ads adds patients for high-value treatments once those basics are in place.

It depends on your goals and market. Start by working out what a new patient is worth over a year, then decide how much you can pay to win one. Track cost per new patient by channel and move budget to what works.

Can dentists use patient testimonials in marketing?

Yes, with care. In the US you generally need the patient's written authorization to use their health information in marketing, and testimonials must be real and not paid for being positive.

Should a dental practice hire a marketing agency?

An agency makes sense when you lack the time or skills in-house. Ask for clear reporting on new patients, ownership of your ad accounts and website, and a written scope with no long lock-in.

title: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) Explained for Small Businesses
seoTitle: Generative Engine Optimization: Simple 2026 Guide
excerpt: Generative engine optimization (GEO) explained: how AI answers pick sources, what Google says about AI Overviews and steps that make pages easy to cite.
content:
Generative engine optimization, or GEO, means making your content easy for AI answer engines to find, understand and cite. Tools such as Google's AI Overviews, ChatGPT search and Perplexity write an answer and link a handful of sources. GEO is about being one of those sources. This guide explains how it works, what Google itself says and the practical steps that help a small business get cited.

Key takeaways

  • GEO builds on SEO: AI answers mostly draw on pages that are already crawlable, indexed and trusted.
  • Clear answers, facts with sources and well-structured pages are easier for AI tools to quote.
  • Google says there are no extra requirements or special files needed to appear in AI Overviews.

What generative engine optimization means

Traditional search shows a list of links. Generative engines write an answer first and cite sources inside or beside it. The term "generative engine optimization" comes from a 2023 research paper by Aggarwal and colleagues, later accepted at the KDD 2024 conference. In their tests, methods such as adding citations, quotations and statistics improved a source's visibility in AI answers by up to 40%, with results varying by topic.

For a business, the goal is simple: when someone asks an AI tool a question in your field, your page should be the clearest, most trustworthy answer it can find.

GEO vs SEO

They overlap far more than they differ. A page that is slow, blocked from crawling or thin will not do well in either.

What Google says about AI Overviews

Google's guidance on AI features and your website is clear on several points:

  • There are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode. A page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet.
  • You do not need new machine-readable files, special "AI text files" or new markup for Google.
  • Normal SEO basics apply: allow crawling, use internal links, offer a good page experience and keep structured data consistent with the visible text.
  • Clicks from AI features are counted in Search Console's Performance report under the "Web" search type.

So, for Google, generative engine optimization is mostly good SEO done well. Other AI tools have their own crawlers, so check that your site does not block the ones you want.

How to optimize for AI answers

  1. Answer the question first. Put a direct, two or three sentence answer at the top of the page or section.
  2. Use clear headings that match how people ask: "How much does a roof repair cost in Denver?"
  3. Back claims with sources. Cite official data and original research, and add the date you checked it.
  4. Add specific facts. Prices, steps, timelines and examples are easier to quote than general claims.
  5. Use structured data that matches the page, such as Organization, LocalBusiness, Article and FAQ. Our free schema markup generator helps.
  6. Show who is behind the content. Author names, credentials, an about page and real contact details build trust.
  7. Keep pages fresh. Update prices, rules and screenshots at least once a year.
  8. Earn mentions elsewhere. Reviews, local press and industry directories help AI tools trust your brand.

Do you need an llms.txt file?

An llms.txt file is a short summary of your site's most useful pages, written for AI tools. Google says it does not need one, and support among other AI tools is uneven. It is cheap to add and harmless, so some sites publish one as a simple map. Our free llms.txt generator builds one in minutes. Do not expect it to replace good pages.

Generative AI in marketing: use it carefully

Generative AI can help draft outlines, summaries and first versions of pages. But AI tools favor accurate, specific, trustworthy sources. Content written by AI and published without checks tends to be generic, and it can contain errors. Use AI for speed and people for facts and judgment. Our guide to AI marketing tools shows a safe workflow with human approval.

How to measure GEO

  • Search Console: watch impressions and clicks for question-style queries.
  • Referral traffic: check analytics for visits from AI tools such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Copilot and Gemini.
  • Manual checks: ask AI tools your main customer questions each month and note who gets cited.
  • Brand searches: a rise in people searching your name can follow AI mentions.

Frequently asked questions

What is generative engine optimization?

Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the practice of making your content easy for AI answer engines to find, understand and cite. It builds on SEO with a focus on clear answers, evidence and trust.

Is GEO different from SEO?

It overlaps heavily. Google says pages need no special work beyond being indexed and eligible for snippets. The difference is focus: GEO pays extra attention to quotable answers, sources and brand trust.

How do I get my business into Google's AI Overviews?

Make sure your pages can be crawled and indexed, answer common questions clearly, keep structured data accurate and build trust with reviews and real business details. Google does not offer a way to request inclusion.

Does AI search reduce website traffic?

It can reduce clicks for simple questions that the answer fully covers. Google says clicks from AI Overviews tend to be higher quality. Pages with depth, tools, prices and local details still earn visits.

Yes. Every SEMRS SEO plan includes GEO work: answer-first structure, schema and content AI tools can quote. See our SEO services and pricing.

Website builders for small business let you launch a professional site without writing code. The main choices are WordPress, Wix, Squarespace and Shopify, and each suits a different kind of business. The four main options

WordPress is free, open-source software that you install on your own hosting. It runs about 38% of all websites, according to W3Techs, and offers thousands of themes and plugins. You own the files and can move hosts at any time.

Wix is a hosted, drag-and-drop builder. Hosting, security and updates are included in the plan. It is easy for beginners and has apps for bookings, stores and events.

How to choose a website builder

  2. Count the pages and features you need in the next two years, not just today.

A Google Ads agency plans, builds and manages your paid search campaigns so you get more leads or sales for your budget. A good one sets up tracking, cuts wasted spend and reports results in plain words. A poor one can lock you into contracts, hide data and judge success by clicks. This guide explains what agencies do, how they charge and the nine questions to ask before you sign.

Key takeaways

  • Insist that the ad account is in your name, with your card paying Google directly.
  • Ask how the agency tracks leads and sales; reports should show cost per lead, not just clicks.
  • Compare fees in dollars at your real budget, and avoid long lock-in contracts.

What a Google Ads agency does

  • Sets up tracking for calls, forms, bookings and sales before spending.
  • Researches keywords and builds campaigns around services and areas.
  • Writes ads and recommends landing page changes.
  • Manages bids and budgets, adding negative keywords to cut waste.
  • Tests ads, offers and pages over time.
  • Reports results and next steps each month.

When to hire an agency, and when not to

An agency makes sense when ads are a main source of customers, your budget is large enough that waste hurts, or you do not have the time to check campaigns every week. If you spend a small amount and have time to learn, managing your own account can work. Our Google Ads for small business guide explains the basics.

How Google Ads agencies charge

Some agencies also charge a setup fee. Always ask for the fee in dollars at your real budget. For example, SEMRS charges 15% of each platform's ad spend, with a minimum of $30 a month per platform, and your card pays Google directly. Our guide to Google Ads cost helps you plan the ad budget itself.

What Google Partner status means

The Google Partners badge shows that an agency meets Google's current requirements. According to Google's help page, these include an optimization score of at least 70% on its manager account, at least $10,000 in ad spend across managed accounts over 90 days and certified staff. It is a useful sign of activity and training, but it does not prove results for a business like yours. Ask for the agency's approach and references too.

9 questions to ask a Google Ads agency

  1. Who owns the ad account? It should be in your name, with admin access for you.
  2. How will you track leads and sales? Expect call, form and booking tracking before launch.
  3. What do you charge, in dollars, at my budget? Get setup and monthly fees in writing.
  4. How long is the contract? Monthly terms with notice are fairer than a one-year lock-in.
  5. Who will manage my account? Ask about their experience and how many accounts they run.
  6. What will you do in the first 90 days? A clear plan beats vague promises.

  8. How do you handle Google's recommendations? Good agencies review each one, not accept all.
  9. Can you share examples from similar businesses? Ask for real, checkable examples.

Red flags to avoid

  • Guaranteed rankings or results. No one controls Google's auction.
  • The agency owns your account. If you leave, you may lose your data and history.
  • Hidden ad spend. You should see exactly what Google charged.

Marketing automation software sends the right message at the right time without you doing it by hand. It can welcome new subscribers, follow up on enquiries, remind customers to book again and pass hot leads to sales. For a small business, the goal is not more email. It is fewer missed follow-ups. This guide covers what these tools do, which features matter, how pricing works and the first automations to set up.

  • Start with a few simple automations: a welcome series, enquiry follow-up and review requests.
  • Choose software that connects to your CRM, website forms and store, so contact data stays in one place.
  • Collect clear consent, and follow email and text message rules in every automation.

What marketing automation software does

Marketing automation software runs actions when a trigger happens. A trigger can be a form submission, a purchase, a date or a click. The action can be an email, a text, a tag, a task for your team or a change in the contact's stage.

Common uses for small businesses:

  • Welcome series for new subscribers.
  • Lead follow-up after a quote request or booking.
  • Abandoned cart emails for online stores.
  • Review requests after a job is finished.
  • Re-booking reminders for services people repeat, such as cleaning or dental checkups.

Features that matter for a small business

How pricing works

Most tools charge by the number of contacts, the number of emails sent or the number of users. Many have free plans with basic email automation; full multi-step workflows often need a higher plan. HubSpot is one example: in November 2026, its Marketing Hub had a free plan with simple email automation, a Starter plan from $20 per seat a month and a Professional plan with full workflows from $800 a month plus a one-time $3,000 onboarding fee.

The lesson: price the plan that includes the automation you actually need, at the list size you expect next year. Our guide to email marketing platforms compares free plans for email-first tools.

Five automations to set up first

  1. Welcome series. Three to five emails over two weeks: thank you, who you are, your most useful guide, a customer story and a clear offer.

  3. Review request. A short email or text a day after the job, with a direct review link. Our free Google review link generator makes the link.

How to choose marketing automation software

Email and text message rules

Automation sends more messages, so compliance matters more. In the US, commercial email must follow the FTC's CAN-SPAM rules: honest headers and subject lines, your postal address and a working unsubscribe that is honored within 10 business days. Marketing texts are stricter. Under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, you generally need the person's prior express written consent before sending automated marketing texts. Using AI in automation

Email marketing sends campaigns to a list. Marketing automation runs flows triggered by each person's actions, and it can include texts, tasks and CRM updates as well as email.

title: Keyword Research for Beginners: A Simple Process with Free Tools
seoTitle: Keyword Research for Beginners: 6 Easy Steps (2026)
excerpt: Keyword research for beginners in six simple steps: find what customers search, judge intent and difficulty, and map one keyword to each page with free tools.
content:
Keyword research is how you find the words your customers type into Google before they buy. It tells you which pages to write, what to call them and which questions to answer. You do not need expensive tools to start. This guide walks through a six-step process for beginners, using free tools and your own customer knowledge.

Key takeaways

  • Start from your services and real customer questions, then use tools to expand and check them.
  • Match each keyword to the search intent behind it: learning, comparing or buying.
  • Give every page one main keyword, and never target the same keyword on two pages.

What keyword research is and why it matters

A keyword is the phrase someone searches for, such as "emergency plumber Denver" or "how much does a website cost". Keyword research finds the phrases that bring the right visitors, not just the most visitors. A local bakery gains little from ranking for "bread", but a lot from "custom birthday cakes Austin".

Good research saves months of writing pages nobody searches for. It also shapes your site structure: each important search gets its own page.

A 6-step process

1. List your seed topics

Write down your services, products, locations and the questions customers ask on calls. Read your emails and reviews. Customers' own words are often better keywords than the words used inside your business.

2. Expand your list with free tools

  • Google search suggestions: type a seed word and note the suggestions and the "People also ask" box.
  • Google Search Console: the Performance report shows the searches that already bring people to your site, with clicks, impressions and average position.
  • Google Keyword Planner: shows estimated monthly searches and ideas. It sits inside Google Ads and needs account setup with billing details, but you do not have to run ads.
  • The SEMRS keyword ideas generator: a free tool that expands one seed into many related ideas.

3. Check the search intent

Search the keyword yourself and look at the top results. They show what Google thinks people want.

If the top results are all guides, a sales page will struggle to rank, and the reverse is true too.

4. Judge difficulty honestly

Look at who ranks now. If the first page is full of national brands and big publishers, pick a more specific phrase. Longer phrases, such as "SEO for dental practices in Ohio", usually have fewer searches but less competition and clearer intent.

5. Map one keyword to each page

Give every page one main keyword and a few close variations. Two pages targeting the same keyword compete with each other. A simple spreadsheet works: keyword, intent, page address and status.

6. Track and update

After publishing, watch the page in Search Console. If it gets impressions for phrases you did not plan, add a section that answers them. Our guide to SEO for small business shows how keyword work fits the rest of SEO.

SEO keyword research mistakes to avoid

  • Chasing volume only. A small, specific keyword that brings buyers beats a big one that brings browsers.
  • Ignoring intent. Writing a blog post for a keyword where people want to buy rarely works.
  • Keyword stuffing. Repeating the phrase makes pages worse. Use it naturally, with synonyms.
  • One page for everything. Each service and location deserves its own page.
  • Never revisiting. Search habits change, and AI answers now cover many simple questions.

Keywords for AI search

AI answers in Google and chat tools draw on pages that clearly answer specific questions. Question keywords, such as "how long does a roof replacement take", are worth a clear, direct answer near the top of a page. What is keyword research in SEO?

It is finding the phrases people search for that match what you offer, then choosing which ones each page should target. It guides what you write and how you structure your site.

Can I do keyword research for free?

Yes. Google's search suggestions, Search Console and Keyword Planner are free to use, and the SEMRS keyword ideas generator is free too. Paid tools add more data, but beginners can get far without them.

How many keywords should a page target?

One main keyword per page, plus close variations and related questions that fit naturally. Do not target the same main keyword on two pages.

How often should I do keyword research?

Do a full round when you plan new pages, and check Search Console every month or two for new questions people use to find you.

title: Business Line of Credit vs Term Loan for Marketing Budgets
seoTitle: Business Line of Credit: Smart 2026 Guide for Marketing
excerpt: How a business line of credit works, how it compares with a term loan for marketing budgets, what lenders check and the costs to compare before you sign.
content:
A business line of credit gives you access to a set amount of money that you can draw, repay and draw again, paying interest only on what you use. That makes it a flexible way to fund marketing that changes month to month. This guide explains how it works, how it compares with a term loan, what lenders check and what it costs.

Key takeaways

  • A line of credit suits ongoing or uneven costs; a term loan suits one large project with a clear payback.
  • Compare the full cost: rate, draw fees, annual fees and whether the rate is variable.
  • Borrow for marketing only when you can track what it earns and repay from that income.

This article is general information, not financial advice. Rates, terms and eligibility vary by lender, so read the full agreement and consider speaking with an accountant before you borrow.

How a business line of credit works

The lender approves a credit limit, say $50,000. You draw money when you need it, up to that limit. You pay interest only on the amount you have drawn. As you repay, the money becomes available again. Many lines have a draw period, after which you repay any balance, and the lender reviews the line each year.

Lines can be unsecured or secured by assets such as receivables or inventory. Secured lines are often larger and cheaper. Most small business lines also need a personal guarantee from the owner.

Line of credit vs term loan

For marketing, the choice depends on the spending pattern. Monthly ad budgets that rise in busy seasons fit a line of credit. A one-off website project with a clear cost fits a term loan, because the fixed payments match a fixed project. Our guide to small business loans for marketing covers term loans in detail.

Where to get a line of credit

  • Your bank or credit union: often the lowest rates if you have a track record and good credit.
  • Online lenders: faster decisions and looser requirements, usually at higher cost.
  • SBA-backed lines: the SBA's 7(a) Working Capital Pilot offers monitored lines of credit of up to $5 million with terms of up to 60 months, for businesses with at least a year of operating history. They are offered through participating lenders.
  • Business credit cards: a simple revolving line for smaller amounts. Our guide to the best business credit cards for ad spend compares the types.

What lenders check

  1. Time in business, often at least one or two years.
  2. Revenue and cash flow, from bank statements and tax returns.
  3. Personal and business credit history.
  4. Existing debt and how much of your income it uses.
  5. Collateral, for secured lines.
  6. Financial statements, such as a profit and loss statement and balance sheet.

Prepare these before you apply. Clean, up-to-date books speed up the decision.

Costs to compare

  • Interest rate: fixed or variable, and what it is tied to.
  • Draw fees: some lenders charge each time you draw.
  • Annual or maintenance fees.
  • Origination fees when the line opens.
  • Prepayment rules and any penalty.
  • Renewal terms: what happens at the yearly review.

Ask each lender for the total cost of a sample draw, such as $10,000 for six months. That makes offers easy to compare.

Using credit for marketing wisely

Borrowed money should fund marketing you can measure. Before you draw:

  • Set up tracking so you can see leads and sales from each channel. Our free ROAS calculator shows the return on ad spend.
  • Start with proven channels and test new ones with small amounts.
  • Plan the repayment from the revenue the campaign brings, not from hope.
  • Set a limit for marketing draws so the line stays available for emergencies.

Our guide to digital marketing cost helps you set a realistic budget.

What is a business line of credit?

It is a revolving credit limit that a business can draw from, repay and draw again. You pay interest only on the amount you use.

Is a line of credit better than a loan for marketing?

A line of credit suits ongoing or seasonal marketing costs. A term loan suits a single large project with a known cost, such as a new website.

How hard is it to get a line of credit for a business?

It depends on your time in business, revenue, credit and debt. Banks usually ask for more history; online lenders approve faster at higher cost.

Does a line of credit need a personal guarantee?

Most small business lines do. That means you are personally responsible if the business cannot repay.

Med spa marketing has two jobs: bring in new clients for treatments such as injectables, laser and skin care, and keep them coming back. This article is general information, not legal or medical advice. Med spas are regulated by state medical boards and other rules that vary by state, so check with your medical director or a healthcare attorney before you advertise treatments.

7 ways to grow a med spa

1. Complete your Google Business Profile

Choose the most accurate main category, list every treatment, add real photos of your rooms and team, and keep hours current. Our Google Business Profile guide covers each field.

2. Build one page per treatment

Clients search for "Botox in Scottsdale" or "laser hair removal near me", not "aesthetic services". Give each main treatment its own page with what it is, who it suits, what to expect, downtime, price ranges or "from" prices, and who performs it. Name the licensed provider and medical director.

3. Earn steady reviews

Ask happy clients for a review after their follow-up visit, with a direct link. Reply calmly and generally, without confirming anyone is a client. Never buy reviews or reward only positive ones.

4. Show real, typical results

Before-and-after photos sell, but only real, unedited photos of your own clients, with their written permission, should be used. Show typical results and include the number of sessions. Avoid filters and lighting changes between photos.

5. Run targeted ads for high-value treatments

Search ads catch people ready to book. Social ads on Instagram and Facebook build interest for newer treatments. Keep claims modest, send each ad to its treatment page and track bookings, not likes. Our guide to Google Ads for small business explains the setup.

Monthly memberships, treatment packages and rebooking reminders turn one-time clients into regulars. Use email and text reminders with clear consent. Our guide to marketing automation software shows simple flows to set up.

7. Share helpful content on social media

Short videos that explain treatments, aftercare and myths build trust. Introduce your providers. Keep claims accurate in posts and captions too.

Med spa digital marketing budget

Advertising and privacy rules

Truthful claims. The FTC's guidance on health products says health benefit claims need competent and reliable scientific evidence. Testimonials and before-and-after images make claims of their own, so they must reflect typical results. A small "results not typical" note does not fix a misleading ad.

Patient privacy. In the US, using a client's health information, including identifiable photos and stories, in marketing generally needs their written authorization under HIPAA. Get signed consent for every photo and testimonial, and store it.

Reviews. The FTC's Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule bans fake reviews and rewarding only positive ones. Staff reviews must disclose the relationship.

State rules. Many states limit who can perform and advertise injectables and laser treatments, and how. Check your state's medical board rules with your medical director.

Choosing a med spa marketing agency

If you hire help, ask for: ad accounts and website in your name, reports on bookings and cost per new client, experience with healthcare advertising rules and a contract you can leave with notice. Avoid anyone who promises guaranteed results.

For most med spas, a complete Google Business Profile, strong reviews and a page for each treatment bring the most bookings for the least money. Ads and memberships add growth once those basics work.

How do med spas get more clients?

They show up in local search, prove results with real before-and-after photos, earn reviews, and keep clients with memberships and rebooking reminders.

Can med spas use before-and-after photos?

Yes, with the client's written permission, and only real, typical, unedited results. Check your state's rules too.

title: Merchant Services for Small Business: Fees and How to Choose
seoTitle: Merchant Services: 6 Smart Checks on Fees in 2026
excerpt: Merchant services explained for small business: how card processing works, pricing models, real published fees and the checks to run before you sign a contract.
content:
Merchant services are the tools and accounts that let your business accept card and digital payments, in person and online. Choosing a provider affects every sale you make, because fees come out of each transaction. This guide explains how card processing works, the main pricing models, real published fees and the checks to run before you sign.

Key takeaways

  • Compare the effective rate: total fees divided by total card sales, not the headline rate.
  • Flat-rate providers are simple for small volumes; interchange-plus pricing often costs less as volume grows.
  • Read contracts for terms, early termination fees and equipment leases before you sign.

This article is general information, not financial advice. Fees and terms change often, so check each provider's current pricing and contract before you sign.

How card processing works

When a customer pays by card, several parties take part:

  1. Your payment terminal or checkout sends the card details securely.
  2. The processor and acquiring bank pass the transaction to the card network.
  3. The card network (such as Visa or Mastercard) routes it to the customer's bank.
  4. The issuing bank approves or declines it.
  5. Funds are settled to your account, minus fees, usually within one to two business days.

Fees go to the card issuer (interchange), the network (assessments) and your provider (markup).

Merchant services pricing models

Published fees from popular providers

These are standard US rates published on the providers' pricing pages in November 2026:

  • Square (Free plan): 2.6% + 15¢ in person, 3.3% + 30¢ online, with no monthly fee.
  • Stripe: 2.9% + 30¢ for online cards, 2.7% + 5¢ in person, plus extra for international cards and currency conversion.

On a $100 sale, that means about $2.75 to $3.60 in fees, depending on the provider and how the card is taken. Online and manually keyed payments usually cost more because the risk of fraud is higher. Larger businesses can often negotiate lower rates.

Fees to look for in the contract

  • Monthly or account fees.
  • Chargeback fees when a customer disputes a payment.
  • PCI compliance fees or non-compliance penalties.
  • Equipment costs: buying a terminal is usually cheaper than a long lease.
  • Early termination fees for leaving before the contract ends.
  • Minimum monthly processing requirements.

Ask for a full fee schedule in writing. If a provider will not give one, look elsewhere.

How to choose merchant services

  1. Work out your volume: monthly card sales, average sale size and how many are online.
  2. Calculate your effective rate from a recent statement: total fees divided by total card sales.
  3. Get quotes in the same format, using your real numbers.
  4. Check what you need: in-person terminals, online checkout, invoices, recurring billing.
  5. Check payout speed and holds on funds.
  6. Prefer month-to-month terms without long equipment leases.

Security and compliance

Any business that takes cards must protect card data. The PCI Security Standards Council sets the PCI DSS rules for businesses that store, process or transmit card data. Most small businesses meet them by using a provider whose terminals and checkout keep card data off their own systems, and by completing the yearly self-assessment their provider asks for.

Accepting payments on your website

If you sell online, your checkout is part of your website. Make it fast, mobile-friendly and simple. Our guide to website builders for small business explains which platforms handle payments well, and our guide to website design cost covers e-commerce budgets.

Frequently asked questions

What are merchant services?

Merchant services are the accounts, tools and processing that let a business accept card and digital payments. They include payment terminals, online checkout and the merchant account that receives the money.

How much do merchant services cost a small business?

You usually pay a percentage of each card sale plus a small fixed fee. In November 2026, published flat rates from Square and Stripe ranged from 2.6% + 15¢ in person to 3.3% + 30¢ online. Check each provider's current rates and contract.

Is flat-rate or interchange-plus pricing better?

Flat-rate pricing is simpler and often fine for small volumes. Interchange-plus usually costs less as volume grows, because you pay the real card costs plus a set markup.

Can I avoid long merchant service contracts?

Yes. Many providers offer month-to-month terms with no early termination fee. Read the contract before signing, and avoid long equipment leases.

This article is general information, not legal advice. Insurance advertising and telemarketing rules vary by state, so check with your state insurance department and compliance team before you run campaigns.

Buying life insurance leads vs generating your own

If you buy, ask whether leads are exclusive or shared, how old they are, how consent was collected and whether you can return bad leads. Test a small batch before committing.

7 ways to generate your own life insurance leads

1. Ask for referrals

Happy clients and their families are your best source. Ask at policy delivery and at each review. Partner with financial planners, accountants and estate attorneys who serve the same people.

2. Get found in local search

Many people search "life insurance agent near me". A complete Google Business Profile with reviews puts you on the map. Our Google Business Profile guide shows how.

3. Publish helpful content

Answer real questions: "How much life insurance do I need?" or "Term vs whole life for a young family". Helpful pages bring searchers who are already thinking about cover.

4. Market around life events

Marriage, a new baby, a new home and a new business all raise the need for cover. Reach these people through content, partners such as mortgage brokers and realtors, and targeted ads.

5. Run search ads

Search ads reach people actively looking. Keep them tight by product and area, and send them to a matching page with a quote form. Our guide to Google Ads for small business covers the setup.

Follow up fast

Contact and advertising rules

Do Not Call. The FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule requires sellers to check their calling lists against the National Do Not Call Registry at least every 31 days. Calls are allowed only between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. local time. An established business relationship exception lasts 18 months after a purchase or three months after an inquiry.

Texts and automated calls. Marketing texts and robocalls generally need the person's prior express written consent under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act. Keep a record of how and when each lead gave consent.

Advertising. State insurance departments regulate insurance ads. Name the insurer where required, avoid misleading comparisons and keep a copy of every ad.

Referrals, a Google Business Profile, helpful content and community events cost little money. They take time and steady effort.

  • Never pay, give discounts for reviews or ask only happy customers; Google and the FTC ban it.
  • Reply to every review, good or bad, calmly and without sharing private details.

Why Google reviews matter

Google's local ranking help page says prominence is one of the main factors in local results, and the number of reviews and their ratings are part of it. Reviews also influence the click: people compare stars, read recent comments and check how the owner replies.

7 ways to get more Google reviews

1. Ask every customer

The simplest step is the one most businesses skip. Google's own tips say to remind customers to leave reviews. Make it part of your process, not an afterthought.

2. Ask at the right moment

Ask when the job is done and the customer is pleased: when a repair is finished, at checkout, or after a good follow-up visit.

3. Send a direct review link

A direct link opens the review box straight away. Our free Google review link generator creates one for your business. Send it by text or email on the same day.

4. Use a QR code in person

Put a QR code on receipts, invoices, the counter or a small card. Google's tips mention customers can scan a QR code to leave a review.

5. Make it part of your follow-up emails

Add a short review request to your thank-you email. Our guide to marketing automation software shows how to send it automatically after each job.

6. Train your team

Staff who know why reviews matter ask naturally. Give them a short script: "If you were happy with us today, a Google review really helps a small business like ours."

7. Reply to every review

Replies show future customers you care. Google's tips recommend replying to reviews. Thank people by name if they used it, and answer complaints calmly with a way to talk offline.

What Google and the FTC do not allow

Google's policy on fake engagement says businesses must not offer incentives or selectively ask for positive reviews. The FTC's rule, in force since October 21, 2024, bans fake reviews and rewards tied to positive reviews.

How to handle negative Google reviews

  • Reply calmly within a few days. Apologize for the experience without admitting legal fault.
  • Take it offline: give a name and a phone number or email.

  • Fix the cause if the complaint is fair.
  • Report reviews that break Google's policies, such as spam, offensive content or reviews from people who were never customers. You can flag them from your Business Profile.

You cannot delete a genuine review just because it is negative. A mix of reviews often looks more trustworthy than a perfect score.

Where to see your reviews

Open your Google Business Profile while signed in, or search for your business name on Google or Maps. Reviews appear in your profile, where you can reply. Our Google Business Profile guide covers the rest of your profile.

Ask every customer at the moment they are happy, send a direct review link the same day, use a QR code in person and reply to every review.

Can I offer a discount for a Google review?

No. Google does not allow incentives for reviews, and FTC rules ban rewards tied to positive reviews.

Can I remove a bad Google review?

Only reviews that break Google's policies can be removed, by reporting them. Genuine negative reviews stay, so reply calmly and fix the issue.

Trigger terms and the APR. Under Regulation Z (12 CFR 1026.24), if an ad states a rate, it must state it as an annual percentage rate (APR). Two ways to use the Google Keyword Planner tool

Discover new keywords is best for brainstorming. Enter a few seed words, such as "boiler repair" and "boiler service", and set the location to the area you serve. Entering a competitor's page address shows the themes Google connects with it.

Get search volume and forecasts is best when you already have a list. Paste your keywords and download the results to a spreadsheet.

How to read the numbers

  • Average monthly searches: an estimate, which may be shown as a range (for example 1K–10K) in accounts with little ad spend. Use it to compare keywords, not as an exact count.
  • Three-month and year-over-year change: shows rising or seasonal topics.
  • Competition: how many advertisers bid on the keyword. It is about ads, not how hard the keyword is to rank for in organic search.
  • Top of page bid (low and high range): what advertisers have paid to appear at the top. Higher bids usually mean the searcher is closer to buying.

Always set the location and language to match your customers. National numbers can mislead a local business.

Turn Keyword Planner data into an SEO plan

  1. Group close variants into one topic. "Boiler repair cost" and "boiler repair price" belong on one page.
  2. Check search intent by searching the keyword yourself and looking at the top results.
  3. Pick one main keyword per page. Our guide to keyword research explains how to map keywords to pages.
  4. Start with specific, lower-competition topics you can realistically rank for.
  5. Track results in Google Search Console, which shows the real searches your pages appear for.

Using Keyword Planner for Google Ads

For ads, focus on keywords with clear buying intent and a top-of-page bid you can afford. Our guide to Google Ads for small business shows how to build your first campaign, and our guide to Google Ads cost explains how to set a budget from the value of a customer.

Free alternatives and helpers

Frequently asked questions

Yes. There is no charge to use it, but you need a Google Ads account with billing details entered. You do not have to run or pay for ads.

Why does Keyword Planner show ranges instead of exact volumes?

Accounts with little or no ad spend may see search volumes as ranges. Use them to compare keywords; the relative size is what matters for planning.

Yes, for ideas and search volumes. Its competition score is about advertisers, so check the search results to judge how hard a keyword is to rank for.

title: Website Redesign: A Step-by-Step Plan That Keeps Your Rankings
seoTitle: Website Redesign: 9 Simple Steps to Avoid Mistakes
excerpt: A website redesign plan in nine steps: goals, content audit, URL mapping, redirects, testing and launch, so you improve the site without losing search traffic.
content:
A website redesign can bring more leads, a faster site and a stronger brand, but a careless one can wipe out years of search traffic overnight. The difference is planning: knowing which pages bring visitors, keeping their addresses or redirecting them, and testing before launch. This guide walks through the process in nine steps.

Key takeaways

  • Start with goals and data: which pages bring traffic and leads today.
  • Map every old URL to a new one and set permanent (301) redirects; Google advises keeping them for at least a year.
  • Test speed, mobile layout, forms and tracking on a staging copy before you launch.

Signs you need a website redesign

  • The site is slow or hard to use on phones.
  • Visitors arrive but few call, book or buy.
  • Your services, prices or brand have changed.
  • The site is hard to update without a developer.
  • It fails basic accessibility checks or looks out of date next to competitors.

If only one or two of these apply, targeted fixes may be cheaper than a full redesign.

The website redesign process in 9 steps

1. Set goals you can measure

"More leads from the website" becomes "20 quote requests a month". Clear goals guide every design choice.

2. Audit your current site

Export your pages and their traffic from Google Search Console and analytics. Note which pages bring visitors, rank for important searches or earn links. These pages must survive the redesign.

3. Decide what stays, changes or goes

4. Plan the structure and content

Sketch the menu and page list. Write or update content before design starts, so the design fits real text.

5. Map old URLs to new URLs

Google's guide to moving a site recommends a mapping of every old URL to its new URL. Keep addresses the same where you can. Where they change, the map becomes your redirect list.

6. Design and build on a staging site

Build on a private copy, not the live site. Check that it works on phones, loads fast and is easy to read. Our ADA website compliance guide covers accessibility basics.

7. Set up 301 redirects

Use server-side permanent redirects (301 or 308) from each old URL to its new match. Google advises keeping redirects for as long as possible, generally at least one year.

8. Test before launch

  • Every form sends and reaches the right inbox.
  • Analytics and conversion tracking work.
  • Old URLs redirect to the right new pages.
  • Titles, meta descriptions and internal links are in place.
  • The site passes speed checks on mobile.

9. Launch and monitor

Submit your new sitemap in Search Console. Watch traffic, rankings and errors for the next few weeks, and fix broken links quickly.

How much does a website redesign cost?

A redesign usually costs about the same as a new site with the same number of pages, because most of the work is content and design. Our guide to website design cost compares options and lists the running costs to budget for.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Changing URLs without redirects, the most common cause of lost traffic.
  • Deleting pages that ranked because they did not fit the new design.
  • Launching without tracking, so you cannot measure results.
  • Choosing looks over speed, with heavy sliders and large images.
  • Redesigning the platform and content at once without a plan for either.

Should you change platforms during a redesign?

Sometimes it makes sense, for example moving from a hosted builder to WordPress for more control. It adds risk, so plan the URL map and redirects with extra care. Our guide to website builders for small business compares the options.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a website redesign take?

Small business redesigns often take a few weeks to a few months, depending on the number of pages, who writes the content and how quickly decisions are made.

Will a redesign hurt my SEO?

It should not if you keep important URLs or redirect them, keep good content and test before launch. Most traffic losses come from missing redirects or deleted pages.

How long should I keep 301 redirects after a redesign?

Google advises keeping them for as long as possible, generally at least one year.

How often should a business redesign its website?

There is no fixed rule. Redesign when the site no longer meets your goals, works poorly on phones or no longer reflects your business. Many sites only need regular updates in between.

Yes. SEMRS rebuilds sites on WordPress at fixed prices, with URL mapping, redirects, speed and SEO checks included, and you own the site. See our web design services and pricing.

Near me SEO is about showing up when someone searches "plumber near me", "coffee near me" or "dentist open now". These searches come from people who want to act soon, often within the hour. You cannot add "near me" to your pages to rank; Google works out who is near from the searcher's location.   • A complete, accurate Google Business Profile with steady reviews is the biggest lever.
  • Do not stuff "near me" into pages or your business name; use your real service areas instead.

How Google chooses businesses for near me searches

Google's help page on local ranking says results are based mainly on three things:

  • Relevance: how well your business matches the search, based on your categories, services and information.
  • Distance: how far your business is from the searcher or the place in the search.
  • Prominence: how well known your business is, including reviews, ratings, links and mentions across the web.

7 steps to improve near me SEO

2. Keep your hours accurate

3. Earn steady reviews

Ask every happy customer for a review with a direct link, and reply to all reviews. Our guide on how to get more Google reviews shows how to do it within Google's rules.

4. Build pages for the areas you really serve

Create a page for each main town or district you cover, with real local details: jobs you have done there, travel times and local rules. Avoid copying the same page with only the town name changed.

5. Keep your name, address and phone consistent

List your business with the same details on your website, directories and social profiles. Mixed details confuse search engines and customers.

6. Make your site fast on phones

Most nearby searches happen on phones. Show your phone number and a call button at the top of every page, and keep pages light.

7. Add local business schema

Structured data tells search engines your address, hours and services. Our free local business schema generator creates it.

Near me SEO mistakes to avoid

Service area businesses

If you visit customers rather than having them visit you, such as plumbers, cleaners or mobile mechanics, set up a service area profile and hide your home address. Your distance is then judged from your business location, so focus on relevance and prominence for the wider area.

Complete your Google Business Profile, keep hours accurate, earn reviews, build pages for the areas you really serve and keep your details consistent online. Google works out who is near from the searcher's location.

Should I put "near me" on my website?

No. Google does not need it to understand location, and stuffing it into pages or your business name can hurt you. Use your real town and service area names instead.

Can I pay Google to show up in near me results?

You cannot pay for a better local ranking. You can run ads that appear in or above the map results, labeled as ads.

Why does a competitor farther away rank above me?

Distance is only one factor. A competitor with a more relevant profile, more reviews or a stronger online reputation can outrank a closer business.

Google Ads keywords decide which searches can trigger your ads, so they decide where your budget goes. Good keywords bring people ready to call, book or buy. Key takeaways

  • Start with phrase and exact match, then widen only when you have conversion data.

What makes a good Google Ads keyword

The best keywords match what you sell, where you sell it and when someone is ready to act.

How to choose Google Ads keywords in 7 steps

  1. List your services and locations. Each service you want leads for needs its own set of keywords.
  2. Add buying words. Price, cost, quote, near me, book, hire, same day and emergency.
  3. Expand with Keyword Planner. It suggests related keywords, monthly searches and typical bids. Our Google Keyword Planner guide explains how to use it.

Keyword match types

Google's help page lists three match types:

Broad match is the default. It reaches the most searches but spends fastest on loosely related terms. For small budgets, start with phrase and exact match. Try broad match later with smart bidding once conversion tracking has enough data.

Negative keywords

Negative keywords stop your ads from showing on searches that contain them. Google's help page notes that negative keywords do not match close variants, so you need to add synonyms and singular or plural forms yourself.

Common negatives for service businesses:

  • jobs, careers, salary, hiring

Use the search terms report every week

  • Single broad words such as "plumbing" or "insurance".

Phrase and exact match usually waste less money at the start. Broad match can work later with smart bidding and reliable conversion tracking.

title: How to Plan an Email Campaign That Gets Results
seoTitle: Email Campaign Guide: 8 Simple Steps That Get Results
excerpt: How to plan an email campaign step by step: goal, audience, offer, subject line, design, testing and measuring, plus the CAN-SPAM rules to follow.
content:
An email campaign is a planned series of emails with one goal, such as filling a workshop, launching a service or bringing back past customers. Done well, it is one of the cheapest ways to turn your list into sales. This guide shows how to plan one in eight steps, what to write, how to stay out of spam and which rules every sender must follow.

Key takeaways

  • Give each campaign one goal, one audience and one clear call to action.
  • Plan two to four emails over one to three weeks rather than a single send.
  • Follow CAN-SPAM, authenticate your domain and track clicks to your site.

Types of email campaigns

Plan an email campaign in 8 steps

1. Set one goal

"Book 30 boiler services in March" is better than "send a newsletter". The goal decides the audience, offer and success measure.

2. Choose the audience

Send to the people the offer suits: past customers, new subscribers, people who clicked a topic before. Smaller, relevant lists get better results than sending everything to everyone.

3. Shape the offer

Give a reason to act now: a seasonal service, a limited number of slots or a useful guide. Keep it honest; no fake deadlines.

4. Write the sequence

A simple three-email campaign:

  1. Announcement: the offer and why it matters.
  2. Reminder: answer common questions or share a customer story.
  3. Last chance: a short note before the offer ends.

5. Write subject lines that earn the open

Keep subject lines clear and specific: "Your boiler check: 20 slots left for March". Match the subject to the email; misleading subjects break the law and the reader's trust.

6. Design for phones

Use one column, short paragraphs, a large button and alt text on images. Most people read email on their phone.

7. Test before sending

Send a test to yourself, check links, check the mobile view and preview the plain-text version.

8. Send, then measure

Track opens, clicks, replies, unsubscribes and, most important, bookings or sales. Tag links with UTM codes using our free UTM builder so visits show up in your analytics.

Rules you must follow

The FTC's CAN-SPAM guide sets the rules for US commercial email. Every campaign email must:

  • Use accurate "From" details and a subject line that is not deceptive.
  • Identify itself as an ad where it is one.
  • Include a valid postal address.
  • Offer a clear way to opt out, and honor opt-outs within 10 business days.

Google's email sender guidelines also require senders to authenticate their domain. Bulk senders to Gmail must set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC, offer one-click unsubscribe and keep spam complaints low.

Tools to run your campaign

Any good email platform can schedule a sequence, segment your list and report results. Our guide to email marketing platforms compares free plans, and our guide to marketing automation software shows how to run campaigns automatically.

Frequently asked questions

How many emails should an email campaign have?

Most small business campaigns work well with two to four emails over one to three weeks: an announcement, a reminder and a last-chance note.

What is a good click rate?

It varies by industry and list. Compare each campaign with your own past results and focus on bookings or sales, which matter more than opens.

When is the best time to send?

Test with your own list. Many businesses find weekday mornings work, but your audience's habits matter more than general advice.

Do I need permission to send marketing emails?

In the US, CAN-SPAM allows commercial email if you follow its rules, including an easy opt-out. Many other countries require consent first, so collect clear opt-ins.

10 ways to use ChatGPT for marketing

  1. Brainstorm content ideas from customer questions you paste in.

  3. Draft email subject lines and test several versions.
  4. Write ad variations for Google and Meta ads, then edit for accuracy and policy.

So the test is quality: is the page accurate, useful and written with real experience?

The limits of ChatGPT for marketing

Google says appropriate use of AI is not against its guidelines. It acts against content made mainly to manipulate rankings, whatever tool produced it.
