Final expense leads are people, usually older adults, who have asked about small whole life policies that cover funeral and end-of-life costs. Many agents buy these leads, but quality varies widely, and the rules on calling and texting are strict. This guide compares bought and self-generated leads, explains how to judge a vendor and shows seven ways to build your own.

Key takeaways

  • Ask every lead vendor whether leads are exclusive, how fresh they are and how consent was collected.
  • Your own leads, from referrals, local search and community events, cost less over time and convert better.
  • Follow Do Not Call rules, calling hours and consent rules for texts and automated calls.

This article is general information, not legal advice. Insurance marketing and telemarketing rules vary by state, so check with your state insurance department and compliance team.

Types of final expense leads

How to judge a lead vendor

  1. Exclusive or shared? Shared leads go to several agents at once.
  2. How fresh? Ask how quickly leads are delivered after the form is filled in.
  3. How was consent collected? Ask to see the form wording and records.
  4. Return policy: can you return wrong numbers and fake details?
  5. Test small: buy a small batch and track how many become policies.

Compare vendors by cost per policy sold, not cost per lead.

7 ways to build your own leads

  1. Ask for referrals at policy delivery and at annual reviews.
  2. Partner locally with funeral homes, senior centers and churches where allowed.
  3. Complete your Google Business Profile and collect reviews. Our Google Business Profile guide shows how.
  4. Publish helpful content answering questions such as "How much does a funeral cost?" or "Do I need a medical exam for final expense insurance?"
  5. Hold free educational seminars on planning ahead, without pressure selling.
  6. Run search ads for clear-intent phrases. Our guide to Google Ads for small business covers the setup.
  7. Stay in touch with a simple monthly letter or email to clients and their families.

Contact rules every agent must follow

Do Not Call. The FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule requires sellers to check their calling lists against the National Do Not Call Registry at least every 31 days and to call only between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. local time. An established business relationship exception lasts 18 months after a purchase or three months after an inquiry.

Texts and automated calls. Marketing texts and robocalls generally need the person's prior express written consent. Keep records of how and when each lead gave it.

Honest selling to seniors. Explain waiting periods, premiums and benefits clearly, and never pressure a prospect. State insurance departments regulate insurance advertising and sales practices.

Follow up fast and respectfully

Internet leads cool within minutes. Call promptly during allowed hours, introduce yourself clearly and offer to send information. Track every lead in a CRM; our guide to the best CRM for small business explains what to look for.

Our guide to life insurance leads covers more channels for agents.

Frequently asked questions

What are final expense leads?

They are people, usually older adults, who have asked for information about small whole life policies that pay for funeral and end-of-life costs.

title: How to Set an Advertising Budget for a Small Business

  • Start from customer value: how much you can afford to pay to win one customer.
  • Fund one or two channels properly for at least a month before judging them.

Set your advertising budget in 6 steps

1. Work out what a customer is worth

Seasonal budgets

Many businesses have busy and quiet seasons. Spend more when customers are searching, such as heating repairs in winter, and keep a smaller, steady budget in quiet months to stay visible.

There is no single right amount. Work back from what a customer is worth and how many you want each month, then test that budget for at least a month.

Ad spend, management fees, creative costs and tools such as call tracking. Budgeting only for ad spend understates the real cost.

title: Fast Business Funding: Options, Real Costs and Warning Signs
seoTitle: Quick Business Funding: 6 Smart Options and Risks
excerpt: Quick business funding options compared: lines of credit, online loans, invoice financing and cash advances, with real costs and warning signs to watch.
content:
Quick business funding helps when a big order, a repair or a slow month needs cash within days, not weeks. Fast money usually costs more, and some offers hide their true cost behind daily payments and "factor rates". This guide compares the main options for quick business funding, shows how to work out the real cost and lists the warning signs that should make you walk away.

Key takeaways

  • The fastest options usually cost the most; a bank line of credit set up in advance is often the cheapest way to have money ready.
  • Convert every offer to a total cost in dollars and an annual rate before you compare.
  • Walk away from pressure, upfront fees, blank documents or offers that ignore your ability to repay.

This article is general information, not financial advice. Terms vary by lender and change often, so read the full agreement and consider speaking with an accountant before you borrow.

Quick business funding options compared

SBA-backed loans are rarely the fastest, but they are often among the cheapest. The SBA's 7(a) Working Capital Pilot, for example, offers monitored lines of credit for businesses with at least a year of history. Our guide to a business line of credit explains how to set one up before you need it.

How to compare the real cost

Fast funding is often quoted in ways that make it look cheaper than it is:

  • Factor rates: a factor rate of 1.3 on $20,000 means you repay $26,000. That $6,000 cost over a few months is far more expensive than it sounds.
  • Daily or weekly payments: these can strain cash flow, even if the total seems manageable.
  • Fees: origination, processing and early repayment fees all add up.

For every offer, write down:

  1. The amount you receive after fees.
  2. The total you will repay.
  3. How long you have, and how often you pay.
  4. The cost in dollars (total repaid minus amount received).
  5. Whether paying early saves money.

Ask each lender for an annual percentage rate. If they will not give one, be cautious.

Warning signs to walk away from

  • Pressure to sign today.
  • Fees you must pay before you receive the money.
  • Blank spaces in documents you are asked to sign.
  • No questions about your revenue or ability to repay.
  • Unclear answers about the total cost.
  • Requests to sign over control of your bank account without clear limits.

Before you borrow: other ways to find cash

  • Collect faster: send invoices the day work finishes and follow up quickly.
  • Ask suppliers for longer terms.
  • Offer a small discount for early payment to big customers.
  • Cut or pause spending that does not bring revenue.

If the money is for marketing, borrow only for channels you can measure. Our guide to small business loans for marketing explains how to judge the return before you borrow.

Frequently asked questions

What is the fastest way to get business funding?

An existing line of credit or a business credit card is usually fastest. Online lenders and cash advances can fund in days, but usually cost much more.

Is a merchant cash advance a loan?

It is usually structured as a purchase of your future card sales rather than a loan, so it may not come with the same disclosures. Its effective cost is often very high, so compare it carefully.

How do I compare a factor rate with an interest rate?

Work out the total you repay, subtract what you receive and compare that dollar cost over the time you have to repay. Ask the lender for an annual percentage rate as well.

Can I get quick business funding with bad credit?

Some lenders focus on revenue rather than credit, but costs are usually higher. Check the full cost and the repayment schedule before you sign.

Technical SEO makes sure search engines can find, read and index your pages, and that visitors get a fast, secure site. Great content cannot rank if Google cannot reach it. This checklist covers the basics every small business site needs, how to check each one and what to fix first.

Key takeaways

  • Google's minimum requirements: Googlebot is not blocked, the page returns a 200 status and it has indexable content.

How search engines see your site

Search works in layers. Google first crawls a page, then renders it, then decides whether to index it, and only then can it rank it. A problem in a lower layer blocks everything above it.

Google's technical requirements page lists three minimum requirements for a page to be eligible for indexing:

  1. Googlebot is not blocked.
  2. The page works, returning an HTTP 200 (success) status code.
  3. The page has indexable content.

Meeting them does not guarantee indexing, but missing any one of them stops it.

The technical SEO checklist

Fix these first

  1. Pages that should rank but are not indexed. Check robots.txt, noindex tags and canonical tags.
  2. Slow mobile pages. Compress images and remove heavy scripts. Our free image compressor helps.
  3. Redirect chains and broken links after a redesign. Our guide to website redesign explains URL mapping.
  4. Missing or broken sitemap. Most CMSs create one automatically.

Do you need a sitemap?

Google's sitemap guide says a small site, about 500 pages or fewer, may not need one if it is well linked internally. A sitemap still helps new sites with few links, large sites and sites with lots of images or video. Submitting one costs nothing.

WordPress settings to check

WordPress handles many basics, but check:

  • Settings, Reading: "Discourage search engines" must be off on the live site.
  • Permalinks: use readable addresses such as /service-name/.
  • One SEO plugin, not two, to avoid duplicate tags.
  • Updates and backups to keep the site secure.

Technical SEO is the work that lets search engines crawl, render and index your site, and gives visitors a fast, secure, mobile-friendly experience.

Check Search Console monthly and run a fuller audit after a redesign, a platform change or a sudden drop in traffic.

Both matter. Technical work makes pages eligible to rank; helpful content earns the ranking. Fix blocking issues first, then focus on content.

User generated content is any photo, video, review or post that your customers create about your business. It is often more trusted than your own marketing, because it shows real people and real results. Using it well means asking permission, crediting the creator and following the rules on endorsements. This guide shows how to collect it and use it the right way.

Key takeaways

  • Always ask permission before reposting a customer's photo or video, and credit them.

Types of user generated content

  • Reviews on Google and other sites.

  • Social posts that tag or mention your business.
  • Questions and answers from customers in comments or forums.

How to use customer content the right way

  3. Disclose connections. If you gave the person a free product, a discount or payment, say so clearly.

What the FTC says

The FTC's guide to its Endorsement Guides explains that a connection between you and the person posting, such as payment or a free product, should be disclosed clearly when people would not expect it. Even a small incentive can need disclosure if it could affect how people weigh the post. Each new endorsement made without a disclosure could be deceptive.

What to automate (and what not to)

6 sales automation workflows to copy

  1. New lead capture: form or call → contact created in the CRM → owner assigned.
  2. Instant reply: new lead → email or text (with consent) confirming you received the request and when you will call.
  3. Speed-to-lead alert: no call logged within one hour → reminder to the owner and their manager.
  4. Quote follow-up: quote sent → reminder after three days if there is no reply → second reminder after a week.
  5. Appointment reminders: booking confirmed → reminder the day before.
  6. Won or lost: deal closed → review request for won deals, short feedback question for lost ones.

Tools you need

  • A CRM to hold every contact and deal. Our guide to the best CRM for small business explains what to look for.
  • Email and text tools connected to the CRM.
  • Web forms and call tracking that send leads straight into the CRM.

Many CRMs include basic workflows. Our guide to marketing automation software covers tools that add more advanced workflows.

Rules for automated messages

Email. The FTC's CAN-SPAM guide applies to commercial email: accurate headers, honest subject lines, a postal address and an opt-out honored within 10 business days. One-to-one transactional replies, such as confirming a request, have fewer rules, but keep them honest.

Texts and calls. Automated marketing texts and calls generally need the person's prior express written consent under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act. Record when and how each person agreed.

Common mistakes

  • Automating a broken process. Fix the steps first, then automate them.
  • Too many automated messages, which feel like spam and raise unsubscribes.
  • No owner for each lead, so reminders go to nobody.
  • Not testing workflows with a real form before going live.
  • Forgetting to update templates when prices or services change.

Measuring results

Track:

  • Speed to first contact.
  • Lead-to-appointment rate.
  • Quote-to-win rate.
  • Leads with no follow-up (this should fall to zero).

Frequently asked questions

What is sales automation?

Sales automation uses software to handle repetitive sales tasks, such as logging leads, sending first replies, setting reminders and updating deal stages.

What should a small team automate first?

Start with lead capture into a CRM, an instant reply to new enquiries and follow-up reminders. These stop leads from slipping through.

Will automation make my sales feel impersonal?

Not if you automate tasks, not conversations. Use automation to make sure a person calls quickly and follows up on time.

Do I need consent to send automated texts to leads?

For marketing texts, you generally need prior express written consent. Keep records and honor opt-outs.

title: Health Insurance Leads for Agents: Buy, Build and Stay Compliant
seoTitle: Health Insurance Leads: 7 Smart Ways for Agents
excerpt: How agents get health insurance leads: bought vs self-generated leads, seven ways to build your own, and the consent rules for Marketplace enrollment and calls.
content:
Health insurance leads are people who have asked for help choosing a health plan, whether through the Marketplace, an employer group or an individual policy. Agents can buy them or build their own. Either way, the rules are strict: Marketplace agents must document consent, and calls and texts have their own rules. This guide compares the options, shows seven ways to build your own leads and explains the consent rules.

Key takeaways

  • Bought leads are fast but often shared; your own leads cost less over time and trust you more.
  • Marketplace agents must document a consumer's consent before helping, and document that the consumer reviewed the application.
  • Follow Do Not Call rules and get written consent before marketing texts.

This article is general information, not legal or compliance advice. Health insurance marketing rules vary by state and program, so check with your state insurance department, carriers and CMS guidance.

Consent rules for Marketplace agents

CMS's model consent form for Marketplace agents and brokers explains that agents, brokers and web-brokers must document a consumer's consent before helping them enroll, and must document that the consumer reviewed and confirmed their eligibility application before it is submitted.

The model form covers:

  • Who gives consent and who receives it, including the agent's National Producer Number.
  • What the agent may do: search for an application, complete it, help with ongoing maintenance and respond to Marketplace inquiries.
  • How personal information will be used and protected.
  • How long consent lasts and how to revoke it.

CMS says consent can be documented in different formats, such as a recorded call, text, email, an electronic document with a digital signature or a signed paper form.

Buying vs building leads

If you buy, ask how consent was collected, whether leads are exclusive and how fresh they are. Our guide to final expense leads has a full vendor checklist.

7 ways to build your own health insurance leads

  1. Referrals from clients, accountants and HR advisers.
  2. Google Business Profile with reviews, so local searchers find you.
  3. Helpful content that explains plan types, deductibles and enrollment dates.
  4. Employer outreach for small group plans.
  5. Community workshops on choosing a plan, without pressure selling.
  6. Search ads for clear-intent phrases in your licensed states.
  7. Year-round email with reminders before enrollment periods.

Call and text rules

The FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule requires sellers to check their call lists against the National Do Not Call Registry at least every 31 days and to call only between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. local time. Marketing texts and automated calls generally need prior express written consent. Keep records for every lead.

Frequently asked questions

What are health insurance leads?

They are people who have asked for help choosing or buying health coverage, such as a Marketplace plan, an individual policy or a small group plan.

Do Marketplace agents need written consent?

Agents must document the consumer's consent before helping them enroll. CMS allows several formats, including recorded calls, texts, emails, electronic signatures and signed paper forms.

Are bought leads worth it?

They can be if they are fresh, exclusive and properly consented. Test small and compare the cost per policy with your own sources.

How can agents get free health insurance leads?

Referrals, a Google Business Profile, helpful content and community workshops cost little money but take steady effort.

title: Real Estate Listing Marketing That Sells Homes
seoTitle: Listing Marketing: 9 Smart Ideas to Sell Homes Faster
excerpt: Listing marketing for real estate agents: photos, video, descriptions, social, email and open houses, plus the fair housing rules every listing ad must follow.
content:
Listing marketing is everything an agent does to get a home seen by the right buyers: photos, video, the description, social posts, emails, signs and open houses. Strong listing marketing helps a home sell and wins the next seller, who sees how you present properties. This guide covers nine ideas and the fair housing rules every listing ad must follow.

Key takeaways

  • Professional photos and an honest, specific description do most of the work.
  • Promote each listing across portals, social media, email and your own website.
  • Describe the property and area, never the kind of buyer you want; fair housing rules apply to every ad.

This article is general information, not legal advice. Real estate advertising rules vary by state, brokerage and MLS, so check with your broker.

9 listing marketing ideas

  1. Professional photos in good light, with wide but honest angles.
  2. A video walkthrough or short vertical clips for social media.
  3. A floor plan so buyers understand the layout.
  4. A specific description: room sizes, recent updates, natural light and what is nearby.
  5. A property page on your website with all photos, details and a contact form.
  6. Social posts and ads for the listing, using the housing ad category where required.
  7. Email to your buyer list and to agents who sell in the area.
  8. Signs and flyers with a QR code to the property page.
  9. Open houses promoted a week ahead, with follow-up to every visitor.

Writing a listing description

Be specific and accurate, and describe features rather than people.

Fair housing rules for listing ads

The fair housing regulation on discriminatory advertisements (24 CFR 100.75) bans ads that show a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin. That includes words, images and even where ads are placed.

Online ad platforms also limit targeting for housing ads. Google's personalized advertising policy says housing ads in the US and Canada cannot target by age, gender, parental status, marital status or ZIP code. Our guide to real estate advertising covers these rules in more detail.

Measure listing marketing

  • Views and saves on portals.
  • Showing requests and open house visitors.
  • Enquiries from your property page and ads.
  • Days on market compared with similar homes.

Tag every link with UTM codes using our free UTM builder so you can see which channels bring buyers.

Use listings to win sellers

Every listing is also marketing for you. Share before-and-after staging, just-listed and just-sold posts, and a short story of how the home sold. Future sellers notice agents who present homes well.

Frequently asked questions

What is listing marketing?

It is the set of activities that promote a home for sale: photos, video, descriptions, property pages, social media, email, signs and open houses.

What makes a good listing description?

Specific, accurate details about the home and area: room sizes, updates, light and nearby amenities. Avoid describing the kind of buyer you want.

Can I target real estate ads by age or ZIP code?

On Google in the US and Canada, housing ads cannot target by age, gender, parental status, marital status or ZIP code. Meta also requires a special ad category for housing.

Should every listing have its own web page?

Yes, when you can. A property page on your site gives buyers one place for all details and brings enquiries to you.
